claim: On average the VIX over-forecasts the next month's variance: the mean scaled seller payoff is 30.1% of implied variance (95% CI 21.9% to 38.3%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 0.3011 [0.2188, 0.3834] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 7.17, p = 7.3e-13; payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 0.3011 [0.2145, 0.3761] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: The raw variance payoff is positive on average: 0.01112 in annualised variance (95% CI 0.005556 to 0.01669).
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 0.01112 [0.005556, 0.01669] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 3.92, p = 9.0e-05; payoff_var / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 0.01112 [0.004988, 0.01617] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.0005
caveat: Raw variance is dominated by a few crash months; quote it next to the scaled payoff.

claim: The VIX has exceeded the volatility that followed by 4.181 vol points on average (95% CI 3.425 to 4.937).
evidence: vol_spread_pts / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 4.181 [3.425, 4.937] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 10.84, p = 2.2e-27; vol_spread_pts / monthly 1990–2025 / mean: 4.181 [3.383, 4.909] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: The typical (median) month pays the seller 47.5% of implied variance (95% CI 42.8% to 50.7%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / median: 0.475 [0.4278, 0.5071] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), sign test (362/432 positive), p = 1.5e-48

claim: The variance seller wins in 83.8% of months (95% CI 80.0% to 87.0%), far more often than a coin flip.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / win_rate: 0.838 [0.8003, 0.8697] (Wilson (i.i.d.)), exact binomial (362/432), p = 1.5e-48; payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / win_rate: 0.838 [0.7986, 0.8727] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: The scaled payoff is strongly negatively skewed (skewness -5.016, 95% CI -6.159 to -3.69): many small gains, a few huge losses.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / skewness: -5.016 [-6.159, -3.69] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), D'Agostino skewness test (i.i.d.), p = 3.5e-72

claim: The raw variance payoff is negatively skewed (skewness -7.339, 95% CI -11.49 to 0.1281).
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 1990–2025 / skewness: -7.339 [-11.49, 0.1281] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), D'Agostino skewness test (i.i.d.), p = 4.2e-95
fallback: Say: the raw variance payoff has a large negative sample skewness, but it is driven by a few months (the block-bootstrap CI reaches zero), so lead with the scaled payoff's skewness instead.

claim: The payoff has fat tails: excess kurtosis 33.25 (95% CI 17.4 to 53.86; normal = 0).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / excess_kurtosis: 33.25 [17.4, 53.86] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), Anscombe–Glynn kurtosis test (i.i.d.), p = 4.8e-34

claim: The mean sits well below the median (mean − median = -17.4%, 95% CI -24.7% to -10.8%): a long left tail of bad months pulls the average down.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / mean_minus_median: -0.1739 [-0.247, -0.1077] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap (H0: mean = median), p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: Extreme losing months are far more common than a bell curve predicts: 10 months fall more than 3 standard deviations below the mean (95% CI 5.452 to 18.18).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / months_below_mean_minus_3sd: 10 [5.452, 18.18] (Wilson (i.i.d.), in months), exact binomial vs normal tail probability, p = 6.7e-10

claim: The average losing month is larger than the average winning month (|avg loss| / avg gain = 1.549, 95% CI 0.8938 to 2.3).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / loss_to_gain_ratio: 1.549 [0.8938, 2.3] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap (H0: |avg loss| = avg gain), p = 0.13
fallback: Say: the *worst* months are many times the average gain (descriptive facts below), but the *average* loss is not significantly bigger than the average gain. The lopsidedness is in the extreme tail, not the typical loss.

claim: Seller payoffs move with the S&P 500 over the same 21 days (correlation 0.516, 95% CI 0.4432 to 0.582): the seller loses when stocks fall.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / corr_with_spx_fwd21_ret: 0.516 [0.4432, 0.582] (Fisher z (i.i.d.)), Pearson, p = 9.2e-31; payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / corr_with_spx_fwd21_ret: 0.516 [0.4042, 0.6033] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001
caveat: Same-window outcomes: this describes when losses happen, it is not a forecast made at t.

claim: In sell-off months (S&P down more than 5% over the window) the seller loses on average: mean scaled payoff -78.0% (95% CI -127.0% to -29.0%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / mean_in_selloff: -0.7798 [-1.27, -0.2901] (t (i.i.d.)), one-sample t, t = -3.21, p = 0.0025
caveat: Conditioning on an outcome: descriptive, not forecastable at t.

claim: Sell-off months pay the seller 120.4% of implied variance less than other months (95% CI of the gap 72.6% to 174.6%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / diff_mean_selloff_minus_other: -1.204 [-1.746, -0.7259] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), Welch t, t = -4.94, p = 1.2e-05

claim: The worst 10% of S&P months (decile 1) carry 82.6% of all variance-seller losses (95% CI 53.8% to 93.0%); with no clustering they would carry about 10%.
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 1990–2025 / loss_share_in_decile_1: 0.8257 [0.5383, 0.9296] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), permutation (10,000 shuffles; null mean 0.101), p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: It is the direction of the market, not just big moves: the worst S&P decile pays the seller 128.3% of implied variance less than the best decile (decile 10), although both contain large moves (95% CI of the gap 77.3% to 186.6%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 1990–2025 / diff_mean_decile_1_minus_decile_10: -1.283 [-1.866, -0.7733] (bootstrap over the 2 deciles' months), Welch t, t = -5.21, p = 4.4e-06

claim: The VIX is a biased forecast of realised variance: an unbiased forecast (RV = 0 + 1·IV) is rejected (HAC Wald χ² = 16.46).
evidence: variance / monthly 1990–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 16.46, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 0.000266; vol_pct / monthly 1990–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 189.6, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 6.9e-42; log_variance / monthly 1990–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 332.6, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 6.1e-73

claim: In log terms the VIX's bias is a constant over-statement: intercept -0.4573 (95% CI -0.8421 to -0.0726) with a slope not significantly different from 1.
evidence: log_variance / monthly 1990–2025 / intercept_a: -0.4573 [-0.8421, -0.0726] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC z (H0: a = 0), p = 0.0198
caveat: 'Slope not different from 1' is absence of evidence, not proof that b = 1.
fallback: Say: in logs the point estimate suggests a constant proportional over-statement, but it does not survive the multiple-testing correction. Use the joint unbiasedness rejection instead.

claim: The scaled premium is positive in the live-VIX era alone (post-Sept 2003): mean 24.2% (95% CI 12.0% to 36.5%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / post-2003 only (live VIX) / mean: 0.2423 [0.1198, 0.3648] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 3.88, p = 0.000106

claim: The raw variance premium is positive in the live-VIX era alone (post-Sept 2003): mean 0.007642 (95% CI -8.458e-04 to 0.01613).
reasons: post-2003 only (live VIX): CI [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_var / post-2003 only (live VIX) / mean: 0.007642 [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 1.76, p = 0.0776
fallback: Say: since 2003 the raw variance premium is positive but not statistically significant: raw variance is dominated by a few crash months (see the worst-months table). Quote the scaled premium for the post-2003 era instead.

claim: The scaled premium has been smaller since 2003 than before: difference -15.4% (95% CI -29.7% to -1.8%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / post-2003 minus pre-2003 / diff_mean: -0.154 [-0.2972, -0.01753] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), Welch t, t = -2.46, p = 0.0141
caveat: Pre-2003 VIX values are back-calculated, so part of the gap may be measurement, not economics.
fallback: Say: the point estimate is lower after 2003, but the difference is not significant once we correct for multiple testing.

claim: The positive scaled premium survives every robustness check (post-2003, H = 22, demeaned RV, VXO, daily overlapping windows with Newey–West, dropping the worst months).
evidence: payoff_scaled / post-2003 only (live VIX) / mean: 0.2423 [0.1198, 0.3648] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 3.88, p = 0.000106; payoff_scaled / H = 22 trading days / mean: 0.3005 [0.218, 0.3831] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 7.14, p = 9.4e-13; payoff_scaled / demeaned realised variance / mean: 0.2929 [0.2085, 0.3773] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 6.80, p = 1.0e-11; payoff_scaled / VXO instead of VIX (1990–2021) / mean: 0.3057 [0.2214, 0.3899] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 7.11, p = 1.2e-12; payoff_scaled / daily overlapping windows / mean: 0.2818 [0.1917, 0.3719] (Newey–West (30 lags)), HAC t, t = 6.13, p = 9.0e-10; payoff_scaled / excluding worst 5 months / mean: 0.3589 [0.3073, 0.4105] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 13.63, p = 2.6e-42

claim: The positive raw variance premium survives every robustness check.
reasons: post-2003 only (live VIX): CI [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_var / post-2003 only (live VIX) / mean: 0.007642 [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 1.76, p = 0.0776; payoff_var / H = 22 trading days / mean: 0.01128 [0.005837, 0.01672] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 4.06, p = 4.8e-05; payoff_var / demeaned realised variance / mean: 0.01066 [0.004913, 0.01641] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 3.64, p = 0.000277; payoff_var / VXO instead of VIX (1990–2021) / mean: 0.01308 [0.007052, 0.01911] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 4.25, p = 2.1e-05; payoff_var / daily overlapping windows / mean: 0.01124 [0.006823, 0.01565] (Newey–West (30 lags)), HAC t, t = 4.99, p = 6.0e-07; payoff_var / excluding worst 5 months / mean: 0.01592 [0.01247, 0.01938] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 9.03, p = 1.6e-19
fallback: Say: the raw variance premium is significant in most checks, but not in: post-2003 only (live VIX).
